entries.notes: Two halves of one user outcome. Failing to open a managed graph used to flatten 16 typed source classes through one `display` helper, so the refusal the user could see and copy carried source prose — a page path, a note name, a changed-content excerpt — and the frontend redactor was the only thing standing between that and the screen. Core now maps each source class once to a stable `clean_open.*` code and projects tagged JSON, so there is nothing private left to redact. The second half is the one a typed wire is easy to lose: `safeManagedErrorDetail` collapses any brace group to `[details]`, which carries no diagnostic word, so a correctly typed envelope reached Settings and the startup recovery pane as "The command failed without a safe diagnostic detail." It now renders the envelope from its own closed vocabulary, and a payload whose fields are not that vocabulary still takes the sanitizing path. A third half arrived from CI: two crash-schedule oracles used to prove replay stopped AT an injected cut by matching the cut's own sentence in the refusal text. Once the refusal became a source-class code shared by every projection failure, that identification was gone — one oracle went red, and its sibling would have silently weakened had the code simply been substituted for the prose. Both now assert two things: the exact envelope, and, through `turn_replay_cut_was_reached_for_test`, that the cut actually fired. Ask the cut whether it was reached; never ask an error to identify itself.

entries.title: An unsaved edit is not conflicted by a change notification that carries no per-page divergence

tests: src/App.test.tsx::does not conflict a dirty page when the admitted epoch left it unchanged
src/App.test.tsx::still conflicts a dirty page when the stored revision genuinely moved
src/App.test.tsx::still conflicts a dirty page whose file was deleted under it
src/App.test.tsx::leaves an in-flight save alone — its own base_rev guard is the authority
src/App.test.tsx::does not conflict a dirty page on a legacy watcher echo of our own write
src/App.test.tsx::still conflicts a dirty page on a legacy watcher event that really changed it

entries.notes: Martin, managed graph, deployed 263f8c21: editing a block and then moving it up QUICKLY raised the top-bar banner ““Tine” changed on disk (edited elsewhere or synced in). Your unsaved changes weren’t written.” Doing the same slowly did not. No external writer was involved. Root cause: the managed runtime emits sparse-v2-changed (src-tauri/src/watcher.rs) on every completed tick, and the tick (SyncRuntimeTick, crates/tine-core/src/sync_runtime.rs:1448) carries only epoch: u64 — no page, no origin — and fires for AdmittedNoop, which by name changed nothing. handleSparseV2Changed then asked reloadDisposition, which returns "conflict" for isDirty || isConflicted || isSaving, and called markConflict. So a contentless aggregate signal plus a dirty page produced a conflict with nothing compared. The harm is not cosmetic: doSave refuses a conflicted page, so the banner's own claim became true only because of the banner, and it blocked the very save whose base_rev guard would have decided the question correctly. reloadDisposition conflates two judgments — “do not overwrite the in-memory edit” (always right for a dirty page) and “declare a conflict” (needs proof this page diverged). Fix: divergedFromBaseline(name, stored) in persistence.ts compares the stored page's content revision against the editor's baseline across all four quadrants (equal revision = our own echo, not diverged; different revision = diverged; absent with a baseline = deleted under us, diverged; absent with no baseline = never-written page, not diverged). An in-flight save is skipped entirely: its own base_rev guard is the authority and decides against the exact bytes it is writing. The same proof is applied to the legacy watcher path in handleGraphChange, where Tine's save normally suppresses its own echo but a synced/polled graph or a self-write-marker gap can still surface one (see store.upsertPage). Fail-before proven by reverting only the two production files and rerunning the new tests: the three false-conflict tests failed, and the three “still conflicts” guards passed both before and after, so they are not vacuous. Frontend-integration layer: the real-app reproduction depends on watcher timing and was not reproduced natively; the mechanism was reproduced deterministically at the frontend observation boundary. Follow-up not taken here: give the tick page identity and origin in the backend so the frontend does not have to re-derive per-page divergence from a contentless signal, and consider not emitting sparse-v2-changed for AdmittedNoop at all. 2026-08-07 (021e21a8): the backend half, owed since the frontend repair. The watcher emitted sparse-v2-changed for both admitted tick variants, but AdmittedNoop is by construction the drain step that took no completed batch. So a quiet admission woke the frontend with a contentless signal, which is what a dirty page then read as a conflict against nothing. Only AdmittedComplete now reports a change, via a named and unit-tested predicate in core rather than an inline match in the watcher loop. divergedFromBaseline is unchanged and still required: a tick still names no page and carries no origin, so per-page proof remains the authority.

entries.title: Crash reopen of a lived-in managed graph does not re-resolve one whole-graph manifest per page
entries.notes: Martin reported unsafe reopen of his real managed graph spending about 63.6 s in RecoveringPromotedRuntime. The existing managed_crash_reopen_real_graph_manual_benchmark could not see it: it reopens a graph activated seconds earlier, so its oplog holds one generation (195 ms accelerated, 2.5 s forced-full-replay). The missing variable was aged history. managed_crash_reopen_aged_history_manual_benchmark adds it — N accepted saves across N pages, each fully drained so the local journal crosses its compaction threshold repeatedly, then one pending save and an unsafe drop — and reproduces 72.2 s on the 1,046-file anonymized graph. Localization by successive splitting, each step measured rather than inferred: the reopen rebuilds the disposable projection (projection_recovery=rebuilt-preserving-evidence, reason 'SQLite projection files differ from their authenticated checkpoint'), but the rebuild's own SQLite work is under 0.5 s and forensic preservation is 0.16 ms; 99.6% is materialize_accepted_event_with_stats, and inside that 83% is validate_external_record_anchor at about 30 ms per document. Cause: anchor validation needs the manifest per document, and every document of one bootstrap batch names the same source batch, but load_observed_manifest was called per document — cloning a manifest carrying a descriptor per document, or reloading and revalidating the entire retained bootstrap part off disk, once per page. load_archive_document_object then reloaded that same retained part a second time per document and linearly scanned every object in it. Two whole-graph costs per page, so quadratic in graph size. Fixed by memoizing both for the SAME public operation as the existing status/anchor point caches (cleared together in begin_point_operation, bounded at 4 batches, cleared wholesale at the cap because correctness never depends on a hit), plus a document -> CrdtUpdate index built once per memoized part. This memoizes only WHERE a manifest was found, never WHETHER a record matches it: every document still proves its own descriptor content digest and manifest fingerprint. Measured on the same commit pair: 1,046 files 72,229 ms -> 19,751 ms total and 69,911 ms -> 17,390 ms sqlite_open; 350 files 12,230 -> 3,428; 100 files 2,101 -> 874. Anchor validation 31.6 s -> 0.86 s. tine-core release suite 2030 passed with the same 15 pre-existing failures as master (doc::promoted_heading_tests and model::tests::write_highlights_*, all unrelated and failing identically before the change). STILL OPEN, deliberately not claimed fixed here: the remaining cost is superlinear too — per-document scratch LSM lookups in load_external_exact run without a ScratchLookupSession, unlike the bootstrap bulk materializer which threads one; and the reopen still re-materializes about twice the graph because compacted generations replay whole-graph slices (240/453/220/78 pages for eight single-page edits). Also unaddressed: why the projection is invalidated at all after ordinary drained saves. The regression guard is a 45 s tripwire inside the manual benchmark, which is NOT a CI gate; a counter-based assertion that manifest resolutions are bounded per batch rather than per document would be the durable guard. entries.title: Unsafe reopen opens a projection already at the accepted frontier instead of rebuilding the whole graph
entries.notes: Unsafe reopen of a lived-in managed graph rebuilt the ENTIRE SQLite projection even though that projection was already exactly at the oplog's accepted frontier. Established by evidence, not inference: the single rebuild reason string in validate_projection_checkpoint collapsed three independent bindings into one message; split apart, the one that fired was 'checkpoint names a different frontier root'. A field-by-field probe of the two AcceptedFrontierRoot values then showed exactly ONE differing field: scratch_root. Every authenticated field -- acceptance_sequence, document_map_root_digest, batch_map_root_digest, reference_catalog_root, state_digest -- was identical. scratch_root is a run-local address for where THIS process keeps the frontier's maps; next_accepted_frontier_root never hashes it into state_digest, and the type's own doc comment calls it a run-local scratch-store reference. Reopening a graph moves it as a matter of course. Because it sat inside the derived PartialEq and inside canonical_frontier_root_bytes (postcard of the whole struct), it also propagated into every durable identity derived from those bytes -- the projection checkpoint, the materialization stamp, the stored frontier row -- so a correct, up-to-date projection compared unequal to the very frontier it was already at, and recovery could only read that as corruption and answer by discarding the database and replaying the whole accepted history. Fixed by CUTTING the pointer out of identity rather than by making the rebuild faster: a hand-written PartialEq for AcceptedFrontierRoot that compares the authenticated fields only, and canonical_frontier_root_bytes stripping scratch_root so no persisted digest can depend on where this process happened to put things. Measured on the same commit pair, full anonymized 1,046-file graph: total reopen 72,229 ms -> 2,138 ms, sqlite_open 69,911 ms -> 3.1 ms, projection_recovery rebuilt-preserving-evidence -> opened-existing with 0 batches applied and 0 pages materialized. 350 files 12,230 -> 1,261; 100 files 2,101 -> 598. sqlite_open is now flat (about 3-6 ms) at every graph size instead of about n^1.6. Also landed, diagnosis-only: the three checkpoint bindings now report separately, and validate_existing validates the database against its OWN sequence and distinguishes 'behind the oplog' from 'diverged from the oplog' (both still rebuild; they are no longer reported with the same words). A catch-up path that would apply only the missing batches was written and then REMOVED before landing: with the identity cut in place it never runs (applied_batches=0), and shipping an unexercised recovery posture on the data-safety path is the opposite of cutting. Guard: managed_unsafe_reopen_at_the_accepted_frontier_opens_without_rebuilding is a NON-ignored CI test asserting on counters (projection_recovery == opened-existing, 0 applied batches, 0 materialized pages) rather than elapsed time, so a return of the defect fails on any machine. Fail-before proven by reverting ONLY the two production hunks: the gate failed with 'a projection already at the accepted frontier was not opened as-is (reason: SQLite frontier is stale)'. tine-core release suite 2031 passed with exactly the same 15 pre-existing failures as master (failure sets diffed, byte-identical). Note on suite noise: the oplog::local_active ephemeral-retention test family is load-flaky on master too (reproduced on unmodified master under CPU load); the new gate adds contention and raises how often it is seen. STILL OPEN: the remaining 2.1 s is engine_open, not the projection; per-document scratch LSM lookups in load_external_exact still run without a ScratchLookupSession. entries.title: External edits to pages outside journals/ and pages/ reach the open app instead of staying invisible until reopen
entries.notes: Discovery went graph-wide in the #246 fix; watcher event routing did not follow. The OS watch was already installed recursively on the graph ROOT, so events for a page at the root or in a custom folder arrived correctly -- and were then discarded by the reconcile lane, which filtered pending paths against [journals/, pages/] and built its diff snapshot from those two directories only. Such a page was therefore listed at open and never updated again while the app stayed open. Fixed by giving the watcher the same authority discovery uses (GraphTextScope), via Graph::graph_text_watch_relevant / _descend / _could_contain. Fail-before proven by restoring the two pre-fix predicates in place: the snapshot returned only [journals/2026_08_06.md, pages/Page.md] against an expected five, and event routing returned only [pages/Page.md] against an expected three. Conflict copies stay routed (they are not eligible text but must refresh the conflicts panel); excluded trees (assets/, dot-directories, logseq/bak/) stay excluded on both the routing and the force-a-full-scan paths, so dropping an image into assets/ still cannot trigger a graph rescan. Freshness defect only, not write-safety: the pre-debounce write-guard lane always saw every event and stayed fail-closed.

entries.title: A network-share (poll-mode) graph keeps its save-time admission index warm instead of rebuilding the whole graph on every save
entries.notes: When the watcher runs in poll mode (a network share, or TINE_WATCH=poll), every 3 s cycle invalidated the guarded graph-text admission index unconditionally before reconciling. Since a Direct save consults that index and rebuilds it when invalid -- a two-pass byte-retaining walk of the whole graph -- such a user could never hold a warm index and paid a full-graph rebuild on essentially every save. The blanket invalidation was compensating for the poll rescan being narrower than the index (journals/+pages/ vs graph-wide); once REG-EXTERNAL-GRAPH-WIDE-EVENTS-268 widened the rescan to the same scope, the rescan's own result became a complete account of what changed and is published as exact observations instead. Ordering is load-bearing and asserted: the observation happens after the scan and BEFORE any reconcile, so the index is never staler than the scan that produced it -- the same window the inotify callback lane already had, not a wider one. A scan that could not read part of the graph reports itself incomplete and still invalidates. Fail-before proven by restoring the blanket invalidation in place: the quiet-cycle test then reported invalidated: true with complete_builds unchanged at 1.

entries.title: Saving an existing page never captures or reparses the whole graph
entries.notes: Reopened after the reporter confirmed the defect remained in v0.6.91 Direct Files. The diagnostic refusal was `precheck.limit: guarded graph-text identity construction failed: initial shadow peak build memory bound exceeded`; GH #295 independently measured one complete 1,046-file / 16.7 MB capture on every Windows save (roughly 0.9-1.1 s). Root cause was architectural: both existing-target validation and the atomic replacement transaction invoked the complete managed shadow-import admission index. The cut keeps an existing save local: one exact target parse/read, one capability-safe traversal following only portable-equivalent target path components (including case/NFC aliases in ancestor directories), exact file identity and link-count-one checks, and the existing no-replace/retire/restore/fsync protocol. Missing-target creation now uses its separate single-census cached-evidence proof recorded by REG-DIRECT-CREATE-RETAINED-SHADOW-LIMIT-249-266. On the attached #295 graph in release mode, warm save median was 1.13 ms and forcibly invalidated save median 0.98 ms, with complete builds unchanged at one; the prior current-master measurement was 2.75 ms warm and 70 ms invalidated. Structural tests prove exactly one portable traversal, zero graph capture enumerations, one target parse, and no write on portable/hard-link/external-byte conflicts.

entries.title: Creating a Direct Files page does not build the managed shadow-import retained-byte inventory or strand the edit behind precheck.limit
entries.notes: Post-v0.6.92 reporter evidence revoked the complete save/reopen claim for GH #249 without disproving its Windows-safe filename codec: the timestamp page reaches the editor but save fails with the exact diagnostic `precheck.limit: guarded graph-text identity construction failed: initial shadow peak build memory bound exceeded`. GH #266's v0.6.92 Windows trace records the same 12.8-14.2 s refusal three times while instrumented graph open itself takes 18 ms, leaving open/switch blocked for about 41 s and close eventually offering to discard unsaved work. Commit 0394d6e0 correctly cut the complete admission index from existing-target saves, but deliberately left missing-target creation and its atomic writer on the two-pass byte-retaining managed shadow-import capture. The source fix binds the generation-current parsed identity index, exact cached disk revisions, and page-index failures to one capability/no-follow streaming census; creation retains paths, digests, resource identities, and link counts only, applies the retained raw-byte ceiling per file rather than cumulatively, performs no save-time graph parse or retained-byte capture, fails closed without retry, and gives the resulting proof to the exact no-replace publisher. A final streaming census immediately before no-replace publication closes GH #321's external cross-path race without parsing or retaining graph bytes; deterministic hook tests cover both a portable alias and a distinct path claiming the same semantic title. Identity-preserving existing saves advance warm semantic evidence in O(1), while explicit-title identity changes replace it coherently. Creation refuses portable case/NFC target aliases including ancestors, historical graph extensions and arbitrary eligible paths, explicit semantic owners, hard links/resource aliases, symlink parents/leaves, stale same-length retitles, generation changes, and exact-target or cross-path races without changing incumbent or outside bytes. Existing exact-target saves preserve the prior traversal rule: noncolliding siblings under portable-equivalent or symlink ancestor neighbors do not block the save, while a colliding leaf still refuses. A test-only initial-capture charge equal to the parent peak limit proved the parent failed locally with the exact suffix `initial shadow peak build memory bound exceeded`, classifier `precheck.limit`, and no created file; the same armed limit is untouched by the fixed creation path. This construction used generated temporary graph data only. The reversible timestamp codec is exercised in both filename formats. Packaged Windows pass-after remains required before a released Windows claim.

entries.title: A page whose file was replaced with identical content can still be saved instead of stranding the edit
entries.notes: A save proves it is not clobbering someone else's work two ways: base_rev must still match the bytes on disk, AND the file must still be the same physical file read at load. External tools break the second without touching the first -- OneDrive rehydrating a Files-On-Demand placeholder, a Syncthing pull landing identical bytes, cp over a hardlink. Every later save then failed with 'existing page identity changed since load', and BOTH exits from the resulting conflict prompt were dead ends: Keep-mine re-ran the same check and failed too, and Use-disk-version discarded the user's edit. The watcher now re-pins the retained identity when, and only when, the retained revision still matches the bytes now on disk, so the proof it stands on is unchanged. Fail-before proven by disabling the re-pin in place. The control (a replace that also changes the bytes) still conflicts and still writes nothing, and is asserted alongside.

entries.title: A symlink inside the graph does not make every other page unsaveable
entries.notes: One symlink in a descended, non-excluded scope (graph root, pages/, journals/, a custom folder) aborted the save-time admission capture, and because every Direct save takes that capture to answer a filename question, the whole graph became read-only -- the user's OTHER pages could not be saved either. Skipping is what the rest of Tine already does: every traversal is no-follow, the watcher snapshot never descends a symlinked directory, and graph_inventory_entry never admits a symlinked file, so the capture was the only place escalating a non-entity to a fatal error. The shadow-import bootstrap capture still refuses, asserted separately: an import that silently leaves out a file the user considers part of their graph is a worse failure than a refused import. NOTE the audit's own repro for this finding is WRONG -- it used assets/, which is fixed-excluded, so that experiment goes green and would retire a real finding; both halves are asserted in one test so nobody re-runs it. Known bounded gap: a symlink is no longer a member of the portable-key collision group, matching discovery, which never knew about it either.

entries.title: Save failures that a conflict prompt cannot resolve are reported as themselves, not as a content conflict
entries.notes: The backend collapsed EVERY io::ErrorKind::AlreadyExists to the literal string 'conflict', and the frontend recognised a conflict by testing whether the message CONTAINED that substring. A portable-filename collision, a physical-resource alias, a symlink refusal and 'another document owns this page identity' therefore all raised the content-conflict prompt, whose only options are Keep-mine and Use-disk-version -- neither of which can resolve any of them. Choosing either left the page marked conflicted, and a conflicted page silently refuses to save from then on, so the user's page was stranded by an error message. Only a real base-revision conflict carries the 'conflict' contract now; everything else carries its bounded D0 failure code as a stable prefix and falls through to the retryable path. The frontend match is exact rather than substring. Fail-before is structural and asserted directly on the mapping function.

entries.title: A generation change during the Direct creation census fails closed without repeated whole-graph work
entries.notes: The former Direct missing-target admission capture ran two byte-retaining full-graph passes and retried their disagreement, amplifying unrelated concurrent filesystem activity into repeated whole-graph work. Ordinary Direct creation no longer enters that managed shadow-import capture. It performs one capability/no-follow streaming evidence census, binds it to the generation-current cached semantic snapshot, then performs one final streaming census immediately before publication to detect external cross-path races. Neither census parses or retains graph bytes, and disagreement fails closed without retry or mutation. The deterministic generation-change and final-publication hooks prove bounded work and unchanged neighboring bytes.

entries.title: A save failure a retry cannot change is reported once instead of re-running the whole check three times

tests: src/persistence.test.ts::does not retry failures a retry cannot change

entries.notes: scheduleTransientRetry re-ran a failed save at 100 ms and 300 ms before toasting -- three full attempts per dirty page. Each attempt re-runs the whole pre-save admission check, which on a large graph is the expensive part, only to reach the same answer for a failure class that cannot change on retry: a portable-filename collision, a physical-resource alias, a symlink in scope, a non-portable path, a nofollow refusal, a limit breach, or another page already owning the title. #267's 'about a minute, then a red toast' is that multiplier on top of an already slow check. Those classes now report once; genuinely transient ones (precheck.interrupted, identity.changed_since_load, unclassified I/O) still retry. Depends on REG-SAVE-ERROR-MISCLASSIFIED-AS-CONFLICT-001 for the bounded codes that make the distinction possible.

entries.title: Resolving a save conflict with "keep mine" overwrites the file, including after a real external change
entries.notes: force_save_page proved its right to write the pinned file from PageDto.rev, which pageToDto never sets -- ordinary saves carry the load revision in the separate base_rev argument, as the parameter's own comment said. With rev=None the retained-owner check could not hold, so every override failed AlreadyExists 'path-pinned page does not match its captured exact owner', leaving discard-my-edits as the only working exit from the conflict prompt. The suite missed it because every test force-saved a load_named/load_by_path DTO, which does carry rev=Some -- a shape the wire never produces. entries.title: An unclassified save failure reports what happened instead of raising an unresolvable conflict prompt
entries.notes: direct_save_failure_code ended with a catch-all mapping any AlreadyExists to conflict.other, which commands.rs turned into the literal 'conflict' -- the string that raises the keep-mine/use-disk banner. About forty-five other conditions raise AlreadyExists (managed and projection internals, reservation and page-name collisions) for which neither button helps and 'use disk' discards the user's edits; the mapping also replaced the message text, so a failure that had RETAINED those edits under a recovery name arrived as a bare unexplained conflict. conflict.* membership is now decided by naming a condition. entries.title: External changes to a Tine-managed graph reconcile instead of being refused to the retry limit
entries.notes: The drain proves a durable receipt still describes the accepted state by replaying it and comparing intents; the receipt is written WITH authenticated annotations and the replay runs WITHOUT them. plan_exact_source_projection compared whole annotations, whose spans come from two producers with different conventions over the same bytes: marker instrumentation ends a block before its line terminator, block tiling runs to the start of the next block and includes it. One save through the fall-through branch wrote tiling spans into the receipt, which then became the next save's authenticated base and could never match a fresh render, so every later save took the fall-through while the replay always took the rendered route. Now compares identities and lets spans be re-derived. Bisected to 547f8713, which is correct and was NOT reverted. Eight sync_runtime tests were one defect. entries.title: A refused managed save reports the refusal instead of retrying silently forever

tests: src/persistence.test.ts::does not retry failures a retry cannot change

entries.notes: A managed conflict returned 'conflict: {Reason}'. The frontend compares the conflict string exactly, so it matched neither the banner nor any bounded code and fell into the transient-retry path -- retried on a timer, never surfaced, and the user could quit believing the page was written. Now carries a managed.conflict code the frontend treats as permanent, with a message saying to reload. Deliberately not the bare 'conflict': force is hard-refused while managed storage is active, so that banner's only working button would be the one that discards the user's edits. entries.title: A managed rename on Windows refuses to replace a file that appears between the check and the rename
entries.notes: rename_managed_noreplace used renameat2(RENAME_NOREPLACE) on Linux/Android and renameatx_np(RENAME_EXCL) on macOS/BSD, but Dir::rename on Windows -- which cap-std implements with replace semantics, so the one guarantee its name makes was the one Windows did not provide. Now delegates to rename_projection_between_noreplace, which renames an opened DELETE-access handle with FileRenameInformation and ReplaceIfExists=FALSE and rejects filesystems lacking the primitive before retiring the live source name. Compile-verified for x86_64-pc-windows-gnu locally; behaviour is proved by the Windows CI job, so confidence is partial by design. Audit 2026-08-06 M3.

entries.title: A cleanly shut down managed graph never opens again if its disposable SQLite projection is lost or damaged
entries.notes: A Safe (clean-shutdown) reopen used reopen_promoted_local_runtime_existing_projection, which refused a missing or invalid projection instead of rebuilding it, while the crash path already rebuilt the same state. So the tidier lifecycle was the unrecoverable one: deleting the cache (cleared cache directory, sweeper, restore that skipped it) or leaving it unreadable (corruption, schema-version bump) left the graph permanently unopenable, reported to the frontend as Retryable -- a retry button that can never succeed. The projection is a frontier-stamped disposable cache of an authoritative oplog per ADR 0049, so losing it is recoverable by definition. The Safe path now uses reopen_promoted_local_runtime (AllowRebuild) and the existing-only entry point is deleted; ExistingOnly survives only for the same-process handoff, where the projection is held open by this very process. A present, current projection still opens as-is. Fail-before: both tests fail on the parent commit with OpenRefused.

entries.title: Rebuilding a managed graph's projection cost about n^1.6, so a large graph spent minutes on a recovery a small one did in a second
entries.notes: AcceptedRootMaterializer -- the materializer a projection rebuild actually uses -- held no scratch lookup sessions, while BootstrapBulkMaterializer held two. Every document resolution therefore re-walked the scratch LSM from the top, and the LSM grows with the graph, so per-document cost rose with graph size even though the number of document loads stayed linear (2.17, 2.04, 1.96 loads per file at 100/350/1045 files). Measured on the anonymized corpus: 388 ms / 2,214 ms / 14,976 ms, i.e. exponent 1.46 then 1.76, against Martin's stated ceiling of 10 s and truly linear. After giving the materializer the same two root-bound sessions: 271 ms / 796 ms / 2,627 ms, exponent 0.86 then 1.09. Sessions change only how bytes are reached; every record still proves its own anchor, peer counters and direct heads. The guard asserts session hits exceed misses rather than a wall-clock budget, because a small CI fixture is fast whatever the routing -- which is how this went unnoticed. Fail-before: 0 hits, 0 misses over 128 document loads. Catalog maintenance 2026-08-21: references to deleted pre-0.7 runtime-oracle files were removed. Remaining or replacement references name the current clean-runtime semantic contract; the retired implementation is not accepted as release evidence.

entries.title: An unread catalog-root stamp in the page-alias table made two correct builds of the same graph disagree
entries.notes: reference_alias_bindings carried a catalog_root_digest column that every write path set and no read path ever consulted -- both production reads select resolved_page_id filtered by normalized_alias only. Because it sat in the primary key and the row digest, it made an incrementally drained database and a rebuilt one disagree on a page they resolved identically: the drain stamps the catalog root current when the alias was last touched, a rebuild stamps the root it resolved at. Dumped rows confirmed same alias, same ordinal, same resolved page, different stamp, while both databases carried the same materialization_stamp. Column dropped from the table, its primary key, its index and the digested column list; SQLITE_SCHEMA_VERSION 11 -> 12, so each managed graph rebuilds its projection once. The projection's own materialization_stamp already records the catalog root the whole database is at, which is the question anyone actually asks. Fail-before: the upstream tine-storage test formats::format_identity_is_pinned caught the version change immediately, which is what it is for. 2026-08-17 catalog repair: that reference was removed from the coverage list because it names a test in the tine-storage repository and the certification receipt in this checkout lists format constants, not test names, so nothing here could resolve it. The user outcome -- two correct builds of the same graph agreeing -- is covered by ordinary_drained_saves_match_clean_archive_replay_across_rich_shapes, which is in this repository and runs in the release gate.

entries.title: Linked/Unlinked References, search, quick switch, {{query}}, aliases, templates and asset reads work while Tine-managed storage is active
entries.notes: Martin reported "Couldn't load references because the backend request failed." on every page of a managed graph. Root cause was authority, not references: GraphSlot exposed only legacy write authority, so with_graph refused all ~50 read-only commands under managed storage and only six page-path commands worked. Reads now go through with_read_graph, served for managed bindings by a Graph opened with open_derived_read_only over the projected tree. That view fails every graph-text write at admit_managed_text_writer and ensure_write_target, so a misrouted write command errors instead of writing behind the oplog; assets stay writable because assets/ is outside the oplog's document domain. Writes (rename, delete, merge, config setters, conflict resolution) remain refused under managed storage and still need real oplog implementations. 2026-08-17 catalog repair: the with_read_graph / derived-read-graph mechanism described above was later removed -- state.rs::tests::managed_slots_have_no_retained_parsed_graph_fallback now asserts by source scan that it cannot return -- so the two state.rs rows that named it (a_managed_binding_answers_whole_graph_reads_and_still_refuses_writes, a_legacy_binding_serves_reads_through_its_lease) named tests that no longer exist. The command-layer coverage moved to managed_command_surface.rs, which re-derives every graph command's managed routing from the sources themselves: every_graph_command_declares_what_managed_storage_can_do_with_it proves get_backlinks, get_unlinked_refs, list_pages, page_aliases, list_templates and the rest are ManagedRouted rather than legacy-only, and the_refused_surface_is_exactly_the_commands_still_on_the_legacy_authority pins the refused set. That is the same user outcome -- reads work under managed storage -- proved against the current architecture.

entries.title: Advanced Logseq queries bind :inputs [:current-page] positionally without weakening typed date inputs
entries.notes: OG source at 6e7afa8eb040686ff057156ee877193b581dd369 resolves the typed :current-page keyword positionally through current-page-fn and lowercases the page name before query execution. Tine now retains typed AdvancedInput::Date values while binding that one keyword as AdvancedInput::Page, then conservatively lowers only the exact standard [?p :block/name ?current-page] identity joined to one [?b :block/refs ?p] or [?b :block/page ?p] relationship. Ambiguous and unrelated patterns remain visibly unsupported; this does not claim full DataScript joins. Contract-doc delta: none; this is a bounded compatibility extension within the existing partial advanced-query contract.

entries.title: The graph home page round-trips through Logseq-compatible config.edn without replacing other default-home keys
entries.notes: Config.default_home reads only the direct :page entry inside Logseq's :default-home map. Graph::set_default_home_page uses the existing guarded atomic config boundary, preserves sibling keys such as :sidebar, and refuses a malformed/non-map owner without changing its bytes. The frontend gives graph metadata precedence; when no valid graph-owned page exists it attempts to copy the old home.page.<root> app setting, deleting that legacy value only after the graph write succeeds. A refused migration remains usable for the current session and is retried later. Contract-doc delta: none; ADR 0004 and ADR 0049 already establish config.edn as the compatible graph owner outside the managed oplog domain.

entries.title: Every Settings toggle persists while Tine-managed storage is active
entries.notes: Favorites, preferred workflow, preferred format, journal title format, start of week, show brackets, logical outdenting, doc-mode Enter, time tracking, default journal template and the guide-announced flag all silently failed under Tine-managed storage: the eleven set_* commands went through with_graph, the authority that answers "may this caller write graph text", and a managed binding correctly says no. Settled from source that graph configuration is NOT oplog-owned: the reconciliation scanner classifies logseq/config.edn as GraphTextScanPathClass::Configuration (model.rs, capture_reconciliation_scan_pass) and reconciliation_baseline_adapter.rs::scan_file_row drops those rows as "not managed content" that "cannot be represented as a ManagedPath", so nothing imports, projects or reconciles it; config bytes only join the within-scan two-pass stability digest. sync_runtime.rs:17310, the line that raised the question, is a test fixture's filesystem walk and says nothing about the oplog's domain. Fix: a Graph::ensure_config_write_target capability narrowed to that one exact path, and a with_config_graph route at the command layer. refresh_graph now takes a managed branch that rebuilds the read-only view instead of reopening a legacy graph, because a Graph reads config.edn when it opens. The same branch refreshes the GraphMeta snapshot the slot hands back, which load_graph returns verbatim when a window reloads the root it already holds; without it a saved setting looked reverted on the next load. The legacy path gets that for free by publishing a replacement slot. Still not done under managed storage: set_journal_title_format does not migrate journal filenames, since that is a rename the oplog owns.

entries.title: Orphaned assets can be trashed and the asset trash emptied while Tine-managed storage is active
entries.notes: trash_asset and empty_asset_trash were refused under managed storage only incidentally: the asset itself passed ensure_asset_write_target, but the destination directory went through ensure_write_target, which the read-only view refuses along with graph text. Settled from source that the trash tree is outside the oplog's document domain: graph_text_scope.rs::fixed_excluded lists logseq/.tine-trash beside assets, publish and .tine-sync, so nothing under it is scanned, imported or projected. Fix: Graph::ensure_trash_write_target, used by the four asset-side trash destinations, plus a with_trash_graph route. Page, journal and conflict trashing is unaffected and still refused, because its SOURCE is graph text and it goes through admit_managed_text_writer.

entries.title: Page rename/delete/merge, conflict resolution, guide copy and native capture work while Tine-managed storage is active
entries.notes: Remaining half of the 2026-08-07 authority defect. The read half is REG-MANAGED-WHOLE-GRAPH-READS-REFUSED-001 (25f36f16); settings and the asset trash are REG-MANAGED-SETTINGS-WRITES-REFUSED-001 and REG-MANAGED-ASSET-TRASH-REFUSED-001. Still refused under managed storage, needing real oplog transactions: rename_page, delete_page, merge_pages, rename_file_to_page, resolve_sync_conflict, trash_sync_conflict, trash_journal_file, copy_guide_into_graph. The enumeration this row asked for now exists: src-tauri/src/managed_command_surface.rs lists all 141 Tauri commands with the routing each one uses, re-derives that routing from the sources, and fails when the refused set changes -- so a new command that cannot work under managed storage is a failing diff rather than a user report. That enumeration surfaced a group nobody had listed: publish_html, open_pdf, read_highlights, write_highlights, write_pdf_view_state, save_pdf_area_image, save_asset and stream_asset_path are all asset/publish-domain work, outside the oplog's document domain, still sitting on the legacy write authority. They are the cheapest remaining slice. Tracked as M5 in specs/handoffs/2026-08-06-direct-files-program.md.

entries.title: A managed local journal torn by a crash mid-append can be reopened
entries.notes: KNOWN GAP, quarantined on Martin's call 2026-08-11 rather than held against the 0.6.92 release. tine-storage's v1 journal reader returned FrameRead::TornTail for a partially declared final frame in v0.1.0 and returns CorruptSegment by v0.3.0, per the 2026-08-10 journal-v2 spec requiring a partial frame to fail closed byte-for-byte instead of letting a damaged length field erase a durable commit. The reconciling migration (non-mutating v1 inspection, then rollover to v2) is unfinished, so a crash during an append leaves a managed segment the v1 opener refuses. Managed storage is off by default and testing-only, so no Direct Files user is exposed. Two tests carry the old contract and are #[ignore]d naming GH #308: hot_overlay_tests::torn_final_frame_recovers_and_replays_only_the_complete_prefix (the real gap) and fast_commit::tests::a_torn_final_append_is_recovered_without_losing_earlier_commits (the unwired latency prototype, no user impact). Closing condition is the v2 migration, not loosening the dependency.

entries.title: Undo cannot replay a snapshot recorded against a page instance that was evicted and re-opened

tests: src/store.test.ts::working-set eviction::refuses an undo entry recorded before the page was evicted (GH #305)

entries.notes: Working-set eviction keeps undo history by design, but the kept entry describes the evicted instance. Re-opening installs a fresh instance carrying the file's current content, and invalidateUndoForPage only runs when a load REPLACES a page that is still present, so the stale entry stayed eligible. Replaying it restored pre-eviction content and marked the page dirty; the next save submitted that content under the fresh instance's baseline, which the base-revision guard accepts because the baseline genuinely matches disk, so no conflict was ever raised. Undo/redo entries now carry the page-instance generations they were recorded against and are refused (with the page's history dropped and a toast) when any of those instances is gone. Verified fail-before: the structural-edit repro restored ['keep me','delete me'] over the external content on the unfixed tree.

entries.title: Images and streamed media can be read from nested assets directories
entries.notes: The frontend already reduced ./assets/dir/file.png to the assets-relative name dir/file.png, but all native read entry points applied the top-level-only validator used by asset creation. Read paths now accept ordinary nested relative components and retain canonical containment beneath the approved assets root. Absolute paths, empty/dot/parent components, portable backslash traversal and symlink escapes remain refused. Asset creation/import still accepts only a top-level filename.

entries.title: Opening a large Direct Files graph does not synchronously scan its pages or assets
entries.notes: The reporter measured 44.9 seconds inside the frontend load_graph call on Windows for about 13,000 pages and 25,884 files / 24.6 GB. The representative release benchmark creates 13,000 Markdown pages plus 12,884 sparse assets in 281 buckets (25.2 GiB apparent assets): current core open took 0.4 ms and the full current Linux app returned from load_graph in 65 ms; the released v0.6.90 Linux AppImage returned in 26 ms on the same fixture. Graph size alone therefore did not reproduce the Windows report. The frontend nevertheless performed two optional page-discovery operations synchronously after native binding: default-journal template discovery and configured-home-page lookup. Those may cold-scan a Direct graph and are unnecessary for first interaction. Visible Journals now owns and awaits template materialization before its first feed fetch, preserving #73, while graph open no longer duplicates that work. Configured-home lookup runs in the background and may navigate only if graph, epoch, and landing route are unchanged, so a slow result cannot override user navigation. Frontend phase logs now distinguish native binding, session restoration, and interactivity; native debug logs retain the lower-level phase timings. The Windows scenario and reporter retest remain valuable platform evidence, but the demonstrated synchronous graph-size-dependent frontend work is now removed and its ordering contracts are covered.

entries.title: Managed storage admits parseable non-roundtripping source files byte-exactly and exposes them read-only
entries.notes: The reporter's trace identified the content-specific blocker after source capture: one parseable Markdown file changed block structure under parse/reserialize, and managed import rejected the entire graph even though its error already described the file as byte-preserved and read-only. Tine already admitted the equivalent Org state. Managed import and inactive bootstrap now admit either format as an exact source, while the shared exact-page DTO parser independently recomputes structural editability and marks non-roundtripping Markdown or Org read-only. Existing application/save gates consume that format-neutral flag, so these bytes can be shown but never rewritten. Tests preserve the exact source through both import paths and prove the DTO read-only bit. The UI diagnostic sanitizer now redacts graph-relative source paths while retaining the actual causal reason instead of replacing the whole message with a generic unsafe-detail fallback. The hosted Windows large-graph scenario remains useful platform coverage, but the reporter's demonstrated content cause is now covered deterministically. Catalog maintenance 2026-08-21: references to deleted pre-0.7 runtime-oracle files were removed. Remaining or replacement references name the current clean-runtime semantic contract; the retired implementation is not accepted as release evidence. Lost one bootstrap admission test; the byte-exact parse/identity proof and the Windows real-app journey still cover the stated outcome. Coverage cited here was deleted by the MS-14b managed-storage retirement (9f24d985 detached bootstrap/Patricia, d3707944 enrollment writer residue, 1a3352b0 resume-point residue); the dead references are removed and this note is the audit trail.
