entries.title: Managed activation, reopen, and page switching remain responsive at reporter scale
entries.notes: The original reporter-scale hosted Windows baseline reached 427 seconds: 314 seconds in bootstrap preparation, including 302 seconds of detached authoring, before the intentionally non-roundtripping page produced its expected semantic refusal. The equivalent 13k-page Linux baseline was about 91 seconds. The completed activation redesign reduced successful activation to one live capture plus one final live proof, uses size-adaptive semantic lowering to avoid ordinary graph-sized operation spools, publishes the terminal materialization directly, opens the disposable SQLite projection without replaying accepted history, and keeps page queries bounded. The manual 12k receipt records activation, cold actor open, initial-feed settle, total ready time, and paired Direct Files/Managed Storage logical page-open distributions. Hosted Windows run 33349270671 measured exact-candidate activation at 99.36 seconds but then exposed a separate synthetic 119,990-backlink actor stall; run 33350869828 stopped earlier on an exact-page switcher selector defect. The selector and fixture are corrected, but the two-attempt E2E stop-loss is exhausted and the journey is quarantined pending a fresh unchanged-binary Windows burn-in. The current-only journey still binds the activation executable to the exact candidate by canonical path and SHA-256, force-closes and reopens it, alternates repeated real UI page switches between ordinary and nested Unicode pages in both storage modes, records timing summary statistics, and proves byte-exact return to Direct Files when it completes. Windows responsiveness therefore remains reproduced but not yet covered. Lost the in-memory/spilled builder equivalence test; the scaled activation receipt and the Windows journey still cover the stated outcome. Coverage cited here was deleted by the MS-14b managed-storage retirement (9f24d985 detached bootstrap/Patricia, d3707944 enrollment writer residue, 1a3352b0 resume-point residue); the dead references are removed and this note is the audit trail. Found by the 2026-09-01 debt audit: 13 rows cited 24 deleted tests because check:regressions never ran on landed master (ci.yml had no push trigger).

entries.title: A 20,000-block managed page is admitted without a false memory terminal or thousands of tiny resumptions
entries.notes: The original terminal combined two independent bookkeeping/scheduling defects. Exact-feed preflight accumulated parser estimates and every touched file's raw bytes as though all files were parsed and retained simultaneously; the estimate itself treated every source byte as a node in every parser, DTO, projection, and index allocation class. Preparation is actually serial and retains only the small semantic admission record. Initial construction had the same false parser estimate. Both paths now retain the hard 64 MiB source/batch and 1,000,000 parsed-node caps, check actual retained growth, and account only the currently live file buffer. Separately, the 16-unit coordinator resume budget made fixed reauthentication/reopen overhead dominate and required thousands of turns for one large page. The measured 256-unit bounded slice completes the full 20,000-block external-import and candidate-bounded query regression within its 64-turn contract while still yielding between slices. The regression also proves the sparse query reads the one matching block and its four ancestors rather than hydrating the page. Catalog maintenance 2026-08-21: references to deleted pre-0.7 runtime-oracle files were removed. Remaining or replacement references name the current clean-runtime semantic contract; the retired implementation is not accepted as release evidence.

entries.title: Move up and down crosses child-list edges like Logseq on Android and desktop

tests: src/store.test.ts::cross-day move (journal feed as one list)

entries.notes: Tine's mobile toolbar and desktop editor command already dispatched the same moveBlockFeed operation, but that operation only swapped siblings and stopped at every nested child-list edge. OG uses one shared move-up/down handler too. Its outliner rule swaps ordinary siblings; at a boundary, moving the last child down enters the next parent sibling as its first child, and moving that first child up enters the previous parent sibling as its last child. Tine now implements that same reversible structural rule while retaining root-level journal-feed crossing, subtree identity, inherited list-style semantics, caret-preserving keyed DOM movement, and one undo unit. The regression covers both directions, a child subtree, ordinary sibling movement with Undo/Redo, and the true top boundary.

entries.title: Renaming a page onto an existing page offers the Logseq-compatible complete merge
entries.notes: The previous Tine title editor sent every edit through ordinary rename, whose correct collision guard surfaced only a backend error. OG instead asks whether to merge. The parity behavior is broader than appending two files: Cancel mutates nothing; confirmation appends the source outline after the destination, retains non-conflicting Markdown page properties, rewrites references in the source, destination and every external referrer, renames source namespace descendants to the destination namespace, removes the source, refreshes all open editor state and navigates to the destination. Managed Storage composes the SQLite-indexed exact referrer plan, descendant renames, destination edit and source deletion into one semantic transaction. Direct Files commits the recoverable source-to-trash merge before invoking its existing transactional graph-wide rename/ref rewrite, so a later failure cannot lose either page's bytes. Duplicate-journal merge remains unchanged and never rewrites page identities. Catalog maintenance 2026-08-21: references to deleted pre-0.7 runtime-oracle files were removed. Remaining or replacement references name the current clean-runtime semantic contract; the retired implementation is not accepted as release evidence.

entries.title: A fresh checkout has no tracked paths that collide on a case-insensitive filesystem
entries.notes: docs/UI-REGRESSION-TESTING.md is the current referenced execution contract; the case-only lowercase twin was an older planning document with no references and caused Git to omit one file on Windows checkout. The obsolete twin is removed, and the release-pipeline contract now folds every tracked path through NFC plus lowercase and refuses future collisions.

entries.title: Editing one block does not rewrite bytes belonging to blocks the user never touched
entries.notes: Direct Files data-safety audit 2026-08-09, finding 3, reproduced and re-measured independently: editing one block and reverting it failed to restore the bytes of 96 of 983 files (9.8%) on a copy of ~/research/logseq-anonymized. 88 of the 96 were an unbulleted page-level '## Heading' gaining a '- ' prefix; the worst shape injected the source layout whitespace ('\t  ') into the block TEXT and added a nesting level. Root cause was not the parser: doc.rs's source-layout retention machinery existed but every production call site passed an empty StructuralLayoutIdentity slice, so identity_bound_unbulleted_headings was always empty and the retention was inert on the Direct save path (test-only). doc::layout_identities_of now reads the locator->identity map off the document tree and serialize_page_dto_for_path passes it. Corpus after the fix: 96 damaged -> 0; unchanged-save no-op still byte-exact at 1045/0. Residual, backlogged: a whitespace-only separator line normalises to empty, which is why the continuation-heading test asserts text and depth rather than exact bytes.

entries.title: A content-only save keeps the physical page inventory warm instead of forcing a whole-graph re-read
entries.notes: Direct Files perf audit 2026-08-09, F1, found independently by both the Opus and Codex lanes with agreeing numbers (243 ms vs 263-281 ms). list_pages is memoized on raw cache_gen and its only rebuild path walks the graph text scope, re-reads every file and re-parses each one: ~35 us/file, linear from 506 to 8,006 pages, and find_entry rebuilds straight from it. Every save bumped the generation, so the first navigation or [[ autocomplete after any typing pause stalled ~1/4 s on a real 5,225-file graph. page_list_cache is now re-tagged to the new generation under the same condition the effective-identity index already uses. DELIBERATELY NARROWER than the auditor's recommendation: list_pages parses every file so a title:: edit really does move an entry (hence the !identity_changed gate), and referenced_page_names is genuinely content-derived and is left to rebuild. The test asserts a ratio, not an absolute time, so it survives a loaded shared box.

entries.title: A reference lookup overlapping an ordinary edit waits for its queued one-page SQLite delta instead of scanning the whole graph
entries.notes: GH #400 reported Unlinked References taking one to ten seconds. Direct Files already had a disposable SQLite candidate projection, but every one-page cache publication advanced the parser generation and marked SQLite unavailable until its worker applied the queued delta. A reference request in that short interval immediately used the exact but graph-wide parser fallback. The regression pauses that worker boundary and requires the read to remain pending until the bounded delta converges, while unavailable or failed projections retain the parser fallback. The separate conflict.save_baseline_present event in the report remains an intentional no-write guard for bytes that differ from the editor's loaded revision.

entries.title: Pending edits are written when the app is backgrounded or hidden, not only on a clean window close
entries.notes: Direct Files data-safety audit 2026-08-09, finding 7. The ONLY durability barrier in the app was onCloseRequested. Android/iOS never send one - the OS backgrounds the app and reclaims it later - so everything inside the 400ms save debounce was RAM-only. The three pre-existing visibilitychange listeners (Page.tsx, journal.ts, assetRefresh.ts) all act on becoming VISIBLE; this is the other edge. FAIL-BEFORE is an absence, not a wrong value: no listener flushed on hide, verified by grep across the tree, so there is no pre-fix test that can fail. Confidence for #255 is therefore MODERATE, not high: this is the plainest explanation for the Android half and is a real missing handler, but no same-platform reproduction of the reporter's loss exists. Findings 2 and 6 are other live candidates for the same report.

entries.title: A dirty page name with no page behind it no longer wedges every later flush
entries.notes: Direct Files data-safety audit 2026-08-09, finding 6. doSave bailed on a null DTO BEFORE dirty.delete(name), so the name stayed dirty forever and flushAll() could never return true again: every graph switch aborted with 'Some pages couldn't be saved' and every window close offered to discard edits that were already on disk. Reachable because pinnedPages() did not pin in-flight saves - doSave removes a page from dirty before awaiting, so the working-set cap could evict it mid-write, and a transient failure then re-added a name with no page. Two parts: savingPages() is now pinned (prevents the eviction outright), and a dirty name with no page in the store is dropped rather than wedging. Deliberately NOT dropped when the page exists but the page-header firewall refused the DTO - that is a real unsaved edit and must keep blocking.

entries.title: A watcher-driven disk reload re-checks safety at the moment it applies, not before its IPC
entries.notes: Direct Files data-safety audit 2026-08-09, finding 5. reloadDisposition is correct, but all four watcher sites read its verdict and then awaited backend().getPage(...) before acting - tens to hundreds of ms on a large graph, and a Syncthing burst fires many concurrently. Text typed inside that window was destroyed: upsertPage replaced the page, dropping the edit AND its undo history, with no conflict raised and nothing written to disk. store.upsertUnlessDirty already re-checked at the moment of the upsert; only these sites skipped it. reloadPageIfStillSafe re-checks centrally so a fifth watcher site cannot reintroduce the hole. reloadPage itself is deliberately left as a clobber - 'use disk version' is an explicit user decision.

entries.title: Deleting a page does its graph-wide work on the blocking pool, not the command thread
entries.notes: Direct Files perf audit 2026-08-09, F3. delete_page re-derives the page inventory and rebuilds three O(pages) indexes: measured ~95 us/file, linear, 757 ms at 8,006 files and ~1.9 s projected at 20,000. It was the only such command still running synchronously on the command thread; get_page, save_page and rename_page already cross the blocking pool. The guard test expensive_reference_and_rename_commands_cross_the_blocking_pool existed and simply did not list delete_page - a coverage omission, not a missing mechanism. This does not make delete faster; it stops it freezing command dispatch. The O(graph) cost itself is a separate, still-open finding.

entries.title: An ordinary save after an external atomic replacement compares bytes instead of refusing on physical identity
entries.notes: GH #254 increment 1, ordinary save only. An external editor that writes by temp+rename (the common safe pattern, and what Syncthing/Dropbox deliver) leaves the same path on a NEW inode. save_page authorized with PinnedSaveAuthority::LoadedRevision, whose retained-identity check refused before the byte comparison ever ran, returning 'path-pinned page does not match its captured exact owner' - a message isRetryableSaveFailure retries forever, so the page became permanently unsaveable with no user-resolvable path out. Measured pre-fix: 4 of 5 cases fail, and NOTABLY the different-byte case failed with the same unresolvable code, so a genuine external change was equally unrecoverable, not just the same-byte one. A new authority OrdinaryEditorSave proves exact path ownership and nothing about physical identity; the byte comparison then decides. Equal bytes on a new inode re-pin to the current snapshot and proceed; different bytes return the literal 'conflict' the frontend can resolve. LoadedRevision is UNCHANGED and still used by verify_existing_journal_page_projection, which authenticates before an opaque durable append and must not inherit this reorder - the contract verifier rejected a helper-wide change twice on exactly this boundary. At increment 1, delete conflicts and the force-save half were deliberately deferred to increment 2; the next record covers both.

entries.title: Keep mine writes only over the exact disk snapshot shown by its conflict
entries.notes: GH #254 increment 2. A conflict now mints one per-Graph, per-editor-episode, exact-path, monotonic-epoch token holding Present { revision, resource_identity } or Absent plus the coherently observed baseline bytes. Force consumes it before every attempt and runs the ordinary save protocol with those bytes and identity substituted as its rechecked baseline; it never delegates by revision alone. Under Martin's state-not-events ruling (2026-08-09) a byte-identical republication of the shown snapshot is a no-op, so force DOES rebind to the live inode in exactly that case and refuses a different-byte winner on a new inode; two tests pin both halves. S1-S9 each have a deterministic site test, including both final-reread arms and post-restore/post-publication observation timing. Stable observations get per-site conflict.* codes; exceptional observation failure gets conflict_retry.*, which cannot reach the keep-mine/use-disk banner and now also RETRACTS an existing one: a force has already spent its token by then, so leaving the banner up left Keep-mine permanently dead beside a destructive Use-disk (adversarial implementation verification, finding 3). Loads, watcher observations, forget_file, successful saves, and the shared Tine-owned graph-text mutation boundary revoke authority, covering rename/delete/trash/merge, managed projection/import/migration, sync-conflict resolution, and PDF-highlight page writes. Hard admission refusals remain tokenless.

entries.title: Unlinked References finds a page name written inside code, math and other literal text
entries.notes: Logseq matches unlinked references with a raw regex over the whole block content (db/model.cljs get-page-unlinked-references, only drawer/remove-logbook stripped), so code fences, inline code, math, raw HTML, examples, latex environments and hiccup are all searched. Tine derived its search region from an ALLOWLIST of block kinds in reference_evidence walk_blocks, whose `_ => {}` arm silently dropped every other variant - so the region lost coverage each time lsdoc grew a block type. Now derived by SUBTRACTION: plain_search_ranges takes the complement of what the parser already claimed (explicit refs, block refs, structural properties, :LOGBOOK: drawers), which is Logseq's own semantics reached through the parser rather than a second scanner - alias/NFC/boundary logic unchanged and new lsdoc variants covered for free. Logseq's `#`/doubled-`[` prefix rule had to be ported explicitly (og_prefix_allows): it used to be implied by overlap with a parsed reference, but inside a fence there is no parsed reference, so `[[Page]]` in code would otherwise have matched. That also corrected an inversion - for `\[[Target]]` Tine reported the escaped bracket and hid both code mentions, exactly backwards from Logseq. DELIBERATE DIVERGENCE, named: structural id::/collapsed::/logseq.* property text stays withheld (Logseq scans it) because a page named after a uuid fragment is not a real outcome. PERF: widening the region cost +13% (285->325 ms cold on the 1,045-file anonymized graph), so an ASCII prefilter was added to visit_plain_matches - it skips a start position only when BOTH the name's first char and the source char are ASCII, where lowercase is exact and NFC is identity, leaving folding cases like the Kelvin sign to the authoritative matcher. Net 285 ms -> 36 ms, ~8x faster than before the change. Reusing string buffers instead was measured WORSE (400 ms) because flat_map(char::to_lowercase) loses str::to_lowercase's ASCII fast path. Necessity: 6 unit tests and 2 of 3 integration tests fail on the pre-fix tree; the third asserts the complement did NOT over-widen (an explicit link and a CLOCK: line stay out) and passes both sides.

entries.title: A link naming no existing page is visibly distinguished, and a fileless #tag is not
entries.notes: Martin, 2026-08-09: a generated graph wrote each report to `pages/c01 Swap Bribery.md` with `title:: Swap Bribery` and linked the index by FILENAME. Since Logseq resolves a page's name as title:: > filename > first block (graph-parser extract.cljc get-page-name), the filename named nothing and all 29 links opened blank pages with no signal. Tine <=0.6.5 used the filename and ignored title::; aa4a4b29 (2026-07-29, shipped in 0.6.90) corrected that, which is why the graph looked fine when built. Backend was never at fault - load_named returned full content for all 30 pages. DELIBERATE DIVERGENCE, approved by Martin: Logseq does NOT distinguish unresolved links (components/block.cljs:548 dims only untitled-page?, i.e. a page that EXISTS under a uuid name); Tine dims them, as Obsidian does. Applied to [[refs]] only, NOT #tags - a tag with no page file is ordinary Logseq usage and dimming those would mark most tags in a normal graph. existing_page_names resolves like load_named (normalized keys + alias table, no PageKind filter, so a link to an existing journal is alive) and costs one memoized page-list read per call; pageExistsBatch coalesces every reference in a tick into one IPC, asks each name once per graph, and treats UNKNOWN AS ALIVE so a page of good links never flashes as dead. Verified on the real 30-page graph: 8/8 refs dimmed before the repair, 0/8 after, all six sampled links clicking through to 24-27 block pages.

entries.title: A fluent typing burst is never written to disk until the typist pauses
entries.notes: Direct Files data-safety audit 2026-08-09, finding 9. scheduleSave cleared and re-armed a 400 ms timer on every markDirty, with no ceiling, so the debounce fired only during a pause in typing. Measured fail-before: 40 keystrokes at 300 ms intervals - 12 seconds of prose at a pace slower than most people type - produced ZERO writes. A crash, power loss or OOM kill during a long passage therefore lost the whole passage, and the loss window grew with how well the writing was going. Fixed by measuring a MAX_SAVE_DELAY_MS ceiling of 3 s from the FIRST dirty mark of a burst rather than the last, so the bound is on file staleness rather than typing speed; the burst clock restarts whenever no save is armed, which every drain path (flushAll, resetSaveState, the timer itself) already guarantees by nulling saveTimer. Coalescing is unchanged: a short burst still costs exactly one write.

entries.title: "Use disk version" on a page pinned to a specific file loads a different file
entries.notes: Direct Files data-safety audit 2026-08-09, finding 10. Two files can carry one page NAME - the duplicate-day stray of GH #21, or same-titled pages in different folders - and the editor pins such a page to its exact path so saves write back to the file it was loaded from. ConflictBar's "Use disk version" resolved by NAME (backend getPage), which reaches the backend's canonical owner of that name, so the button silently re-pointed the tab at a different file: the user discarded their edits to THIS file and got someone else's file loaded in its place. Fixed by resolving through getPageByPath whenever the loaded page carries a path - the same idiom store.ts, RightSidebar and LiveRefGroup already use. An absent pinned file drops the page rather than falling back to the name, since that fallback is the same defect; an unpinned (never-saved) page still resolves by name because it has nothing else.

entries.title: Deleting a page with unsaved edits promises a recoverable trash copy that does not contain them
entries.notes: Direct Files data-safety audit 2026-08-09, finding 18. The delete confirmation said only 'The file moves to the graph's .tine-trash folder', which reads as fully recoverable. The trash receives the FILE, so a dirty page's latest keystrokes - and, provably, EVERY edit on a conflicted page, whose saves are refused by design until the conflict is resolved - are destroyed with nothing to recover from. The prompt now names that outcome when the page is dirty or conflicted, while the user can still answer no; wording is unchanged for a page with nothing unsaved. Deliberately NOT fixed by flushing first: making delete trigger a save is a behavior change with its own risk, and it cannot help the conflicted case at all.

entries.title: Closing offers to discard work that is still being written
entries.notes: Direct Files data-safety audit 2026-08-09, finding 11. The shared close transaction (desktop window-close and Android root Back) bounded flushAll at a flat 4 s and treated expiry as failure, so a flush that had merely not FINISHED was reported in the same words as one that could never succeed - 'unsaved changes that couldn't be saved... close anyway and lose them?' - inviting the user to throw away a write in progress. A slow or network filesystem, a fsync behind a busy disk, or many dirty pages can exceed 4 s with nothing wrong; on the 1,045-file anonymized corpus a save averages ~7 ms, so the bound is already several hundred pages' worth. The close now races the SAME flush promise twice: at the soft bound it says 'still saving' and grants a 26 s grace period, and only a flush that genuinely finished false, threw, or outlasted the grace period reaches a discard prompt - which now distinguishes 'failed' from 'still-saving' in its wording. The pre-existing test asserted that the timeout case behaved identically to failure, i.e. it encoded the defect; it was split rather than grandfathered.

entries.title: A conflict raised by a transient file removal is never cleared when the file returns
entries.notes: Direct Files data-safety audit 2026-08-09, finding 17. Raising a conflict was gated on a per-page divergence proof; clearing one was gated on nothing, because only a user's click (or forgetPage) ever cleared a conflict. handleGraphChange's REMOVED branch calls markConflict with no proof at all, so an external editor writing by temp+rename, or a mid-delivery Syncthing pass, could park a page behind the banner permanently. doSave then refuses that page forever, and both banner buttons destroy something: 'Use disk version' the unsaved edit, 'Keep mine' a file it never needed to overwrite. Fixed by making the proof two-directional in ONE owner, applyDivergenceVerdict, used by both observation sites (legacy watcher and sparse-v2 epoch): a negative proof on a currently-conflicted page clears the conflict and reschedules the edit it was freezing. A third site cannot reintroduce the asymmetry. A file that returns with DIFFERENT content still conflicts.

entries.title: The direct shadow-journal rule asked two extensions while its managed twin asked three
entries.notes: Direct Files data-safety audit 2026-08-09, finding 15, landed as a CONSISTENCY fix with an explicit NEGATIVE result. Graph::is_shadow_journal (direct mode) hard-coded canonical candidates '{stem}.md' and '{stem}.org'; its managed twin managed_is_shadow_journal already asked configured_text_variant_paths, i.e. all of LOGSEQ_TEXT_EXTENSIONS = md/markdown/org. The audit predicted that in a '.markdown' graph a title-named leftover would therefore escape the #21 shadow rule and poison the (kind,name) cache. IT DOES NOT: probes at the observation boundary show load_named and journals_desc both still serve the canonical file for both extensions, because later layers mask the misclassification. The necessity gate is therefore NOT satisfied and no user-visible defect is claimed - the divergence between the two classifiers is real and was removed, and the three new tests pin the #21 rule per extension so that a change in whichever layer is currently masking it cannot silently take the guarantee with it.

entries.title: The All Pages sidebar list scanned the whole page list once per visible row
entries.notes: Direct Files performance audit 2026-08-09, finding F9. pageListLabel disambiguates a row whose display name collides with another page (same title in different folders, or the same stem as .md and .org) by scanning the whole list twice - once for the name, once for the parent sub-path. The sidebar called it per rendered row, so rendering All Pages cost O(rows x pages): measured 21 ms at 5,000 pages and 39 ms at 20,000, for 300 visible rows. pageListLabels now counts both keys in ONE pass and returns a lookup, memoized in Sidebar alongside the existing filter+sort memo. The label RULE is unchanged and the three original correctness tests still pass verbatim. Necessity: the shape tests COUNT element reads through a Proxy rather than timing anything - a linear implementation reads the array once while building the index and never again, a per-row scan reads it once more per row - and both fail against the pre-fix implementation. A first attempt asserted wall-clock and was replaced after it flaked on a loaded box: 47 ms against a 26 ms ceiling with the fix in place. The index is keyed by value, not object identity, so a caller holding a copy of an entry gets the same label.

entries.title: Tine crashes at launch with a backtrace when the app-data home is not writable
entries.notes: Found while working the 2026-08-09 Direct Files audit backlog; reproduced on the stock deployed release binary, so not a regression from that work. Tauri creates the WebView user-data directory ($XDG_DATA_HOME/page.tine.Tine) inside its OWN setup(), while building the configured windows (tauri::manager::webview calls create_dir_all there), and an IO error at that point is unreachable by the application: it panics with 'Failed to setup app: Permission denied (os error 13)' at tauri-2.11.2/src/app.rs:1417, before Tine's setup hook runs. A user whose ~/.local/share is root-owned - the shape of the box this was found on, drwxr-xr-t root root - therefore got a hard crash with a backtrace and no actionable message, made more confusing by Tine's own desktop-identity step logging the same Permission denied and explicitly treating it as NON-fatal one line earlier. data_home::ensure_usable now probes the directory before anything resolves it (create_dir_all is not the question: it succeeds on an existing directory nobody may write) and, when it is unusable, points XDG_DATA_HOME at the first writable fallback for that launch - ~/.tine-data, then $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/tine-data, then a uid-namespaced temp dir - so settings, session and the WebView store live somewhere real. XDG_DATA_HOME is the one lever that redirects Tauri's path resolver, WebKitGTK's website-data manager and Tine's own settings together. The frontend toasts once, stickily, naming the directory, because a silent relocation is its own defect. If nothing at all is writable the app prints one actionable sentence and exits 1 rather than panicking. Verified on the built binary: unwritable base -> app stays up, ~/.tine-data/page.tine.Tine populated with tine-settings.json and the WebKit store, nothing written to the read-only base; ordinary writable base -> no relocation diagnostic at all and no probe residue.

entries.title: A graph whose watch() failed stays blind to external changes while another graph is watched
entries.notes: Direct Files data-safety audit 2026-08-09, finding 16, landed in its REACHABLE form only. The audit claimed an inotify watch() failure leaves the watcher permanently blind with no poll fallback; that is not what the code does. A failed root is never inserted into `watched` and is retried on the next cycle, and when EVERY root fails `watched` is empty, which takes the else branch and its bounded <=3 s recv_timeout - a working recovery loop. The reachable case is mixed: with two graphs open, the inotify branch blocks on rx.recv() until an event arrives from a root that IS watched, so a root the kernel refused is retried only when some other graph happens to change. inotify limits are per-user (fs.inotify.max_user_watches), so opening a second large graph is exactly how one root fails while the other is healthy, and on a quiet healthy graph the failing one stays invisible indefinitely. inotify_cycle_wait now bounds the wait to UNWATCHED_ROOT_RETRY (3 s, matching the poll branch ceiling) whenever a desired root is unwatched, and never delays a sooner scheduled retry. Coverage gaps stated in the tests themselves: they pin the wait policy, not a real kernel watch() failure (which needs privileges unavailable here) and not the call-site wiring, and they are a specification rather than fail-before evidence because the function is new.

entries.title: Every typing lull shipped the whole reference-name inventory across IPC
entries.notes: Direct Files performance audit 2026-08-09, finding F7. The frontend's reference-name resource is keyed on dataRev, which a save bumps ~700 ms after every typing lull, so referenced_page_names ran and its result crossed IPC on every pause in typing: measured 15-23 ms and about 5,000 names at 5,225 files, with the JSON parse landing on the UI thread. The answer almost never changes, because typing inside a block rarely adds or removes a [[link]]. referenced_page_names now takes the digest of the set the caller already holds and omits the payload when it still matches, so the ordinary case is an integer. The digest is a commutative fold with the length mixed in: the memo's order comes from a HashMap, so a sequence-dependent hash would report a change on every rebuild and the gate would save nothing. NOT fixed here: the whole-graph recompute itself still runs once per cache generation, because computing the digest needs the names; making it incremental needs per-name reference counts in cache_upsert/cache_remove and is a separate packet. The frontend test pins the dangerous reading of an omitted payload - treating it as an empty set would erase every reference-only page from autocomplete and the namespace tree - and that the digest is actually presented back.

entries.title: Every save case-folded and NFC-normalised every filename in the target's directory
entries.notes: Direct Files performance audit 2026-08-09, finding F6. validate_graph_text_portable_aliases_path_local enumerates each path component's directory looking for case/NFC aliases of the target, and built a PortablePathKey for EVERY entry - a String allocation plus NFD -> default case fold -> NFC per filename. The audit's controlled experiment held graph size constant and varied only layout: 4.87 ms/save with 4,000 pages in one directory versus 0.70 ms with 40 per subdirectory, i.e. 6.9x on layout alone, growing without bound on the one directory that only ever grows (journals/) and running inside the identity-mutation lock. PortablePathKey::graph_text_components_match answers the same question without building either key when both sides are ASCII, where NFD/NFC are the identity and default case folding is exactly ASCII lowercasing. Controlled A/B on this box, same graph and build, 4,000 pages in one directory, 60 saves x 3 runs: 2.54-2.67 ms median before, 1.39-1.41 ms after (~1.8x). The both-sides-ASCII guard is load-bearing rather than redundant: folding can PRODUCE ASCII from non-ASCII (U+212A KELVIN SIGN folds to k, U+FB01 to fi), so a non-ASCII name can legitimately collide with an ASCII one and must still take the full fold. This is an identity boundary whose failure mode is admitting a collision, so the test asserts agreement with the full fold over every ordered pair of a name set that includes NFC/NFD twins, the sharp s, Cyrillic, and both fold-to-ASCII traps. Residual NOT fixed: the directory enumeration is still O(entries); removing that needs the maintained admission index to become the authority for this check, which is a data-safety boundary change and its own packet.

entries.title: A Safe reopen confirms a closed-interval rename before a negative page lookup offers a new draft
entries.notes: Fail-before at 3158cbae: after a Safe handoff, a filesystem rename during the closed interval made the first editor name lookup return NewPage. The startup census correctly found the new file but only staged the old path absence; its post-drain scan is intentionally not independent, so it could acknowledge the queue without admitting the replacement. A negative read now requests one bounded rescan epoch before returning Missing/NewPage. The regression proves the single replacement batch removes the old name and exact path, exposes the new name and exact path with its source content, and leaves no watcher work pending. Catalog maintenance 2026-08-21: references to deleted pre-0.7 runtime-oracle files were removed. Remaining or replacement references name the current clean-runtime semantic contract; the retired implementation is not accepted as release evidence.

entries.title: A duplicated "Keep mine" spent authority minted for a newer winner nobody was shown
entries.notes: GH #254 increment 2, adversarial implementation verification finding 1 (CRITICAL) and the reachable half of finding 2. A force request named its authority only by path plus loaded revision, so consume_conflict_authority could only check SELF-consistency - that the live token is the newest - never that the user had seen it. Reachable data loss with no malicious writer: an external editor or sync client publishes B after the banner showed A; two force requests are in flight under that one banner (the button is not disabled while its request is pending) and the per-page save queue serializes them; the first correctly refuses B and, being a coherent observation, mints fresh authority FOR B; the second, issued before B existed, consumed it and overwrote B. A conflict error now carries the observation epoch it minted at, direct_save_error_message emits it as 'conflict:<n>', the frontend stores it with the banner and echoes it back on force, and consumption requires the presented epoch to equal the live token's. Found while fixing: checking ownership AFTER taking would let one stray duplicate click disarm the banner permanently, so a mis-addressed override is now refused WITHOUT spending the live token - covered by its own test. A force that can name no observation is refused at the command boundary rather than allowed to consume whatever is current. Necessity: all three new core tests fail against the pre-fix check.

entries.title: Managed page and journal deletion preserves the exact accepted projection bytes in typed trash before accepting the tombstone
entries.notes: Accepted managed-storage safety repair, 2026-08-10. An ordinary managed delete derives its exact page ID, accepted path, kind and actor source bytes from one actor turn; durably publishes those exact bytes to logseq/.tine-trash/pages or journals with no overwrite; then re-proves the same actor source, page identity and accepted-frontier root before authoring exactly one DeletePage. H4 adds a retained capability walk from the projection root through logseq, .tine-trash and the typed kind directory: every component is created with ensure_directory_nofollow and reopened with open_dir_nofollow, then tine-storage v0.1.1 publish_immutable_exact publishes or exact-verifies the leaf. On Windows the storage contract is its certified, validated-directory ceiling; it does not claim undocumented power-loss directory fsync. Focused Rust tests cover managed application save followed by exact projected-byte recovery, imported page and journal CRLF/layout, original extension, idempotent unpinned retry, the fresh/malformed typed chain, and a publication failure after optional leaf creation: it refuses before a tombstone or frontier/author advance, leaves the source, and an exact retry converges. Frontend tests cover the bounded page-local quiescence barrier, in-flight second edit, an edit in the resolved-helper handoff, retained save/deferred drafts, and the explicit conflicted-delete path: no draft flush, backend actor invocation, removal only on success, and draft retention on failure. Source-proven fail-before: the prior ordinary DeletePage authored its semantic tombstone without any preservation/re-proof, and its frontend path performed only one dirty flush with no synchronous retirement recheck. Direct Files backend/trash semantics remain unchanged. Catalog maintenance 2026-08-21: references to deleted pre-0.7 runtime-oracle files were removed. Remaining or replacement references name the current clean-runtime semantic contract; the retired implementation is not accepted as release evidence.

entries.title: Unsaved edits were destroyed when a same-named file at a different path was loaded
entries.notes: GH #254 increment 3, contract rule 2. ensurePageLoaded replaced the loaded instance whenever the requested path differed from the incumbent's, with no check that the incumbent held unsaved work. Reproduced: the incumbent's nodes are purged, the dirty mark SURVIVES and now belongs to the replacement's content, and a live conflict banner survives describing a file the editor no longer holds. The gate is the existing reloadDisposition predicate AND an empty editor-lease set - enumerating dirty/conflicted/saving kept losing, because IME composition holds text in the textarea until compositionend and the page-title rename holds its draft in component-local signals, so neither is visible to any store predicate. A component holding uncommitted input now declares itself with a lease keyed by a unique per-component handle, released idempotently from the component lifecycle rather than only from commit/cancel - a lease that outlives its component would refuse every later replacement forever. The gate is re-evaluated synchronously at the final replacement boundary because every caller awaits a backend read first and the incumbent can become dirty during that await. Necessity: both behavioural tests fail against the pre-fix code; the lease-hygiene and clean-replacement cases pass both ways by design and are not regression guards for the refusal itself.

entries.title: Enrollment accepts one canonical keyless current format and fails closed on altered integrity evidence
entries.notes: Pre-0.7 policy has no enrollment migration or compatibility route: unrecognized private state is preserved, Direct Files opens, and current managed state is rebuilt from Markdown/Org. Current authority claims omit secret material; current records use canonical CRC integrity checkpoints. Unknown, old, future, altered, and noncanonical records refuse before lifecycle admission. Crash-cut tests prove old-or-new valid authority, page-boundary audit tests authenticate the current chain, and the source guard proves no legacy schema or authenticator remains. The six stale legacy-migration test references were removed during MS-16 structural closure rather than reintroducing the retired compatibility contract. ZERO surviving coverage. All six cited tests were deleted while oplog/enrollment.rs remains 2,884 lines of live production code, reachable from discovery.rs and object_store.rs, now containing no #[test] at all. The integrity contract in this row's title is currently unproven. Coverage cited here was deleted by the MS-14b managed-storage retirement (9f24d985 detached bootstrap/Patricia, d3707944 enrollment writer residue, 1a3352b0 resume-point residue); the dead references are removed and this note is the audit trail. Found by the 2026-09-01 debt audit: 13 rows cited 24 deleted tests because check:regressions never ran on landed master (ci.yml had no push trigger).

entries.title: Malformed retained scratch no longer permanently refuses an authoritative managed graph

coverage.exemption: Subject machinery retired: the retained-scratch store was removed by the MS-14b managed-storage retirement (scratch_store.rs is absent from the tree), so no code path remains that could reproduce this behavior. Substitute evidence is the retirement source guard check:retired-managed-v1, which fails if retained-scratch production code returns.

entries.notes: A cleanly shut down managed graph selected one retained scratch run through its newest canonical resume point. Deleting only disposable SQLite and corrupting that run's blobs.data reproduced the exact pre-fix terminal result: OpenRefused with 'SQLite materialization failed: immutable archive error: document scratch index failed: malformed scratch blob'. Reopen now recognizes only this typed reconstructible failure, validates the immutable bootstrap authority, preserves the malformed run byte-for-byte, creates a distinct fresh run, fully replays accepted immutable history, and rebuilds SQLite once. The regression proves recovery alone changes neither direct graph bytes nor immutable archive, engine-history, or projection-receipt evidence; then it loads Root.md through the public application API, accepts and reads back a real application save, drains it, proves append-only authority/receipt growth and the updated direct projection, and reaches Safe shutdown. Other malformed or second-attempt errors remain fail-closed. Retired, not regressed: the retained-scratch store was removed with MS-14b (scratch_store.rs absent), so this behavior has no code path left to regress. Coverage cited here was deleted by the MS-14b managed-storage retirement (9f24d985 detached bootstrap/Patricia, d3707944 enrollment writer residue, 1a3352b0 resume-point residue); the dead references are removed and this note is the audit trail. Found by the 2026-09-01 debt audit: 13 rows cited 24 deleted tests because check:regressions never ran on landed master (ci.yml had no push trigger).

entries.title: An in-flight bulk paste never deletes a block the user typed into while it was awaiting, and never lands an insertion the page has meanwhile outgrown
entries.notes: A managed paste caches its decisions during a synchronous preflight and then awaits a cut-source flush and a backend identity lookup. Two facts can change across those awaits. (1) Whether the target is an empty host the paste may REPLACE: if the user types into it while the paste is in flight, replacing it destroys that text. The empty-host decision is now recomputed from the live block at insertion time on both the managed and the Direct path, and the admitted plan assumes the host survives, so the realized block count can only be at or below the admitted one. (2) The page's size and the target's depth: the limit question is re-asked at consumption against the live tree, so an insertion admitted at 510 blocks is refused once the page has reached the cap. Both halves have a literal fail-before proof; before the fix the host block and the text typed into it were deleted outright.

entries.title: The frontend's bulk-insertion byte model is a true lower bound on the native save-request charge, including what the page already holds
entries.notes: The point of admitting a bulk insertion in the frontend is to refuse it BEFORE the page is mutated, so the model must never admit something validate_editor_save_request will reject. It did, two ways. It compared only the INSERTED raw text against the advertised limit, ignoring the page the request also carries, so a small insertion into a nearly full page was admitted and then unsaveable. And it compared with strict greater-than, so an insertion of exactly the advertised byte count was admitted even though the native charge additionally includes the page name/id, the base revision, the preamble and every block's key and parent key, and is therefore necessarily over. The check now sums a bounded census of the existing page (content plus block and parent key bytes, deliberately omitting the page-level terms so the estimate stays a lower bound rather than a guess) with the inserted text, and refuses at the boundary. Fail-before proven by restoring the old comparison: both refusals became admissions.

entries.title: A bulk insertion that selected a storage route synchronously cannot resume onto a different one after its I/O
entries.notes: A file drop reads the storage route once, synchronously, then does its I/O. On the Direct branch that I/O could still be running when the user finished enabling managed storage, and the continuation then inserted an unbounded outline through insertOutlineAfter with no admission at all -- exactly the mutate-first failure the admission work exists to prevent. Graph activation flips this authority inside its own graphTransitioning window, so the existing transitioning check only stopped continuations resuming DURING the switch, not the far more likely ones resuming just after it (a native confirm dialog sits inside that window). The route is now part of the shared continuation fence used by both the drop and the clipboard paste: authority and binding generation are captured with the graph epoch, root, target node, page and page-instance generation, and re-proved before any mutation. The Direct drop also stops reading further files the moment the fence breaks, which additionally removes a TypeError path when the target block was deleted mid-drop. Fail-before proven by removing the fence: the drop imported the asset and inserted.

entries.title: Pasting into a Sheet's cells under managed storage is validated by the storage authority before the live page changes
entries.notes: Sheets have their own clipboard path -- handleSheetPasteEvent -> splatStructuralSheetSelection / pasteTextIntoSheetSelection -- which reached none of preflightManagedBulkInsertion's call sites, so a large CSV/TSV paste materialized an unbounded number of blocks and the limit was only discovered at save time, stranding a partial edit. Resolved not by adding the frontend advisory admission the issue proposed, but by the stronger atomic-plan route: every cell is built in a DETACHED page candidate, the whole resulting page goes to preflight_managed_page_mutation, and the live page, undo history, selection and dirty state change only after the authority accepts. That native preflight applies the real block, depth and byte bounds (validate_application_save_request), so the check is made by the authority itself rather than by a frontend lower bound. Fail-before established at source against v0.6.93, where pasteTextIntoSheetSelection mutated the live document inside withSheetUndo via ensureGridRows/materializeCell/writeCellVisible with no admission and no candidate; that code path no longer exists, so the new test could not be run against it unchanged.

entries.title: A writable page admission does not outlive the evidence that a live actor can save what it admits
entries.notes: sparse-v2-status -- the event carrying applicationPageAdmission -- was emitted only from the watcher's success arm. The Err arm emitted only sparse-v2-error, and suppressed even that when the message repeated, so a persistently failing actor emitted NOTHING after its first error and the last managed_writable admission stayed live indefinitely. Bulk insertions then passed preflight, consumed their token, mutated the page, and had no durable writer: the content is discarded on reload or crash, and the user keeps accumulating edits behind a failure instead of being refused before the first mutation. Two halves. The frontend revokes writability the moment it sees an error, because that is the signal that arrives even when nothing else does; only an authoritative status can restore it, and a tick alone cannot. A Direct admission is left untouched. The watcher additionally asks for status on the failure path and emits it when obtainable, so recovery is decided by the authority rather than by the absence of further errors. The frontend half has a literal fail-before proof; the watcher emit is a source-level change in the tick loop, which has no unit-test seam here.

entries.title: A managed cross-page move resolves from live editor state and resumes the exact durable move after an immediate process loss
entries.notes: The managed move path is one exact, bounded transaction across the source and destination pages. Same-actor resolution first settles the request from the current live editor state; once an episode is durably published, cold recovery resumes that exact episode rather than authoring a replacement. Fault-cut tests cover immediate loss, exact-once completion, external conflict transfer, identity preservation, and bounded work. Catalog maintenance 2026-08-21: references to deleted pre-0.7 runtime-oracle files were removed. Remaining or replacement references name the current clean-runtime semantic contract; the retired implementation is not accepted as release evidence.

entries.title: A corrupt disposable reconciliation baseline is preserved and rebuilt instead of refusing an authoritative managed graph
entries.notes: The reconciliation baseline is derived scheduling state, not authority. Before this repair, any semantic validation failure returned RebuildRequired through both startup call sites and permanently refused the managed graph; the isolated pre-fix test failed at that exact cache boundary. Open now preserves only the four declared baseline files (database/WAL/SHM/journal), completes or resumes the durable evidence move, creates a fresh cache, and marks the rebuild complete only after the replacement opens. Busy/locked/I/O errors stay retryable; symlinks, reparse points and special files remain MS-REF-UNSAFE-FS-KIND refusals and are never moved or followed. Fixed by queueing configuration paths separately (Pending::config_paths) and refreshing the graph when the on-disk bytes differ from those the running Graph was opened with (Graph::open_config_description vs model::config_file_description). That byte gate is mandatory, not an optimization: a refresh discards the whole page cache, and Logseq rewrites config.edn on many ordinary UI actions. The watcher never blocks on the storage transition lane (RefreshLaneWait::TryOnce, deferred and retried) because blocking would stall reconciliation for every graph behind one graph's load or promotion. Configuration is a plain filesystem file under BOTH storage engines - never in GraphTextScope, never in the oplog - so there is one mechanism, not a Direct/managed fork. Fail-before: the pre-fix Pending queue drops an exact config.edn event entirely (incremental_page_paths returns Some(vec![])), which is what the two new watcher tests assert against; before the change config_paths did not exist and the queue was empty for every writer shape. NOT CLOSED: :favorites is still written wholesale from the frontend's snapshot, so a favorite added in Logseq inside the reload window can be overwritten by the next star toggled in Tine; that needs a three-way merge in set_favorites' own atomic_update closure. ALSO FIXED HERE: src-tauri/src/sync_runtime.rs constructed a GraphMeta literal in a test and was never updated when favorites_page was added in b4847dd7, so `cargo test -p tine --lib` did not compile on master. The npm/tsc gates do not build src-tauri tests and the Rust suite compared by name was tine-core, so nothing caught it. SELF-WRITE: a settings write leaves the running graph's parsed view stale (it always has; set_favorites never refreshed it), so the byte gate alone would read every star toggled in the sidebar as an outside change. Graph::write_config is now the single funnel all 13 setters publish through and records what it wrote; the watcher accepts either the open-time digest or that marker. A managed slot retains no Graph to ask, so it re-reads unconditionally and the FRONTEND declines to re-seed favorites it is already showing - fail-before proven by forcing that guard false (the test fails). Also classified set_favorites_page in MANAGED_COMMAND_SURFACE: a third defect from b4847dd7 whose own guard test could not run because the crate did not compile.

entries.title: An ordinary managed edit does not pay a device round trip per archive artifact
entries.notes: Internal report from the 2026-08-26 managed-storage cost-model audit (defect D1), verified by an independent Codex lane and an LD_PRELOAD fsync interposer. User-visible harm: every accepted managed edit blocked on one device round trip per separately durable artifact, so save latency scaled with artifact count rather than edit size - about 20 ms on the audit box's local ext4 and plausibly hundreds of ms on a slow or network filesystem. Classification: blocking stateful UX (latency of the core edit loop), with a data-safety contract attached because the fix changes when bytes become durable. Fail-before on exact base 34e247ac with the new counters: one accepted single-block managed save performed 55 core-initiated durability barriers and one cross-page move 130 (the audit's own broader counter set, which also sees tine-storage-internal barriers, measured 66 and 151 on the 1,045-file anonymized graph). Pass-after: 45 and 109. Two changes: (1) an accepted batch's archive objects and manifest are now staged under temporary names, flushed with ONE syncfs, and only then installed under their final immutable names - ten to sixteen barriers become three; (2) three fsync-before-read helpers on the managed projection paths, which fired three times per save and eight times per move and defended no in-scope failure, are deleted. Crash safety: docs/storage-sync-contract.md section 2.10a-i states the one-durability-point invariant and a crash-point table; clean_batched_archive_publication_leaves_no_torn_immutable_name drives a deterministic cut before the barrier and a second cut mid-install and proves that no immutable name is ever observable with bytes that were never flushed, that the graph still reopens, and that a fresh session completes the same edit. Necessity gate: managed_save_and_move_stay_within_their_barrier_budget fails on the pre-fix code (55 > 45); the mid-install crash test fails against the install-before-flush primitive (tine_storage::ExactImmutablePublicationBatch), which leaves a zero-length immutable object and makes ObjectStore::validate_namespace refuse the whole archive on reopen. Follow-on (P-census, 2026-08-26): the refusal census over the projection receipt store cut the four per-intent namespace binding artifacts - a reservation and an authority for each of attempts/<intent> and forensics/<intent>, four artifacts and eight barriers per projected page - because they detect only a directory renamed or replaced inside Tine's app-private, unsynced, single-writer receipt store, which needs an actor with write access as the user and is out of scope per specs/notes/2026-08-07-trust-model-and-threat-model-decision.md, while a torn or lost 1 KB binding wedged the page's projection permanently. Their refusals became recovery: a missing per-intent recovery namespace is recreated and the drain republishes its byte-identical contents (a_missing_per_intent_recovery_namespace_is_recreated_instead_of_wedging_projection, which fails on the pre-cut code with exactly the removed NamespaceSubstitution refusal). Pass-after: save 37, cross-page move 93, measured identically on the five-file fixture and on a copy of the 1,045-file anonymized graph. Remaining gap to the audit's target of 3/5 is stated in the contract: the projection receipt store's five surviving artifacts per intent, each separated from the next by a read-back and a durable-ordering implication that batching would break (specs/notes/2026-08-26-p-census-receipt.md section 5), and the six projection-directory chain flushes on the user-visible Markdown write path, which neither packet touched. Third packet (P-chain-flush, 2026-08-26, defect D1 continued): the projection directory chain named as the remaining gap above is cut. Every write, rename and preflight on the user-visible Markdown/Org path flushed EVERY directory from the target's parent to the graph root, so a two-deep page paid three device round trips per call and a namespaced page silently cost more than a top-level one. Only the leaf's entry list changes; an ancestor Tine creates is already flushed at creation by create_projection_chain_component, and an ancestor it did not create already has a durable entry in its own parent, which no in-scope scenario can un-durable. Fail-before on exact base d6fd8e03 with the re-pinned budgets: save 37, cross-page move 93, and each of the four new model tests fails on the pre-fix chain walk (for example the depth test observes 15 directory barriers for a three-deep page against 6 for a one-deep one). Pass-after: save 28 (foreground 14 -> 8), cross-page move 77, measured identically on the five-file fixture and on a copy of the 1,045-file anonymized graph. Direct Files uses the same helpers and is covered by a_cross_directory_move_flushes_one_directory_per_side plus the unchanged tests/graph.rs neighborhood. Remaining gap to the audit's target of 3/5 is now only the projection receipt store's five surviving artifacts per intent, plus the six times per save the projection chain is entered at all - which is a publication-protocol question, not a barrier-rule one (specs/notes/2026-08-26-p-chain-flush-receipt.md). MS-05 narrows the original batch-wide safety statement only for the managed-local drain: its undrained journal frame now authorizes exact object repair, while public publication and the manifest remain strict. The separate REG-MANAGED-ARCHIVE-TORN-OBJECT-JOURNAL-REPAIR row carries the replacement crash proof and fail-closed limits. MS-11 makes the Android group-commit fallback host-executable: a simulated syncfs capability refusal flushes every exact staged file, while a real I/O failure stays fatal; focused Android NDK compilation and Windows native CI provide the platform evidence without launching the full matrix.

entries.title: The flight recorder releases its single-writer lock when it is dropped, not when the last forked copy of the descriptor closes

coverage.failBefore: proven — with the Drop impl removed the new test fails with the exact signature the census recorded from the real flakes: Os { code: 11, kind: WouldBlock, message: "Resource temporarily unavailable" }

entries.notes: FlightRecorder held its process.lock in a `_process_lock: File` field with no Drop and no unlock, so release was a side effect of closing that descriptor. An flock belongs to the open file description, not to the descriptor: every process spawn duplicates the description into a child that holds it until exec, so a recorder dropped inside that window left the lock held and the next open on the same directory got EAGAIN. Observed twice in campaign evidence (wave3 I5, wave4 G1) as a first-run failure of the two session-cleanliness tests that then passed on rerun — four extra `cargo test -p tine` invocations in the G1 lane alone, on the gate every lane runs. Drop now calls unlock, which acts on the description and so releases every copy at once.

entries.title: Direct Files indexed queries evaluate only the shared lowering's candidate pages, and abandon the projection when that candidate set is not selective

coverage.failBefore: proven — tine-agents/evidence/wave4/b4b-pass2/. Routing, checked at 9bad907f: every newly routed shape (non-sparse Task, BlockProperty, PageProperty, Page, Namespace, Journal, mixed And, complete Or) left the candidate-read counter unchanged and entered the full-graph evaluator. Hatch, checked at 9bad907f with the cutoff neutralised (hatch-fail-before.log): the unselective plan completed a candidate query instead of abandoning — `an abandoned plan must complete no candidate query, left: 2, right: 1`.

entries.notes: The user outcome: a {{query}} block in Direct mode walked the whole graph after every keystroke even though the projection could answer it. Indexed plans now take the shared Managed/Direct lowering; Empty returns without projection or graph access; All keeps the walk. The lowering returns a page SUPERSET rather than the answer, so an unselective plan names most of the graph and materialising it through SQLite is slower than the walk — measured on the 1,045-file anonymized corpus at 1.08 -> 11.19 ms for non-sparse Task and 0.46 -> 3.31 ms for (journal). A candidate-count escape hatch (more than graph_pages/32, floor 32) therefore abandons the projection and reuses the existing parser-fallback path with a second reason. Both routes return identical groups/total/exceeded. The hatch carries the codebase's first `// RETIREMENT-CANDIDATE:` marker, censused by tests/retirement_candidates.rs; the walk is also the differential correctness oracle for the real lowering that would replace it, so it outlives the hatch.

entries.title: Managed journal-range queries returned nothing when the graph configured a non-default journal page-title format
entries.notes: Direct Files derives a journal page's ordinal from the graph's configured JournalFormat, the producer that fills PageEntry::date_key. The managed query adapters derived it instead from query.rs journal_ordinal, which called JournalDate::from_title and so hardcoded the DEFAULT title format. On any graph whose :journal/page-title-format differs from the default the managed ordinal was None, so every predicate reading a journal day -- (between START END) and the other journal-day forms -- excluded every journal page and the managed query answered empty while Direct answered normally. ApplicationQueryPage now carries the day from the configured format, so one producer serves both backends. The sparse task-candidate path still reads the default format, but symmetrically for both backends (its ApplicationSparseQueryPage is also built in direct_projection.rs), so it cannot diverge; giving it the configured format is a follow-up.

sources.internal: 2026-09 query-engine campaign, packet P0-rust Wave A; found while building the SPEC 3.4 conformance fixture

entries.notes: parse_property_line documents that it returns borrowed slices, and reference_evidence recovers each half's source offset by subtracting the line's base pointer. For a bare key:: with no trailing space the empty value was the static "" literal instead, so the subtraction underflowed and panicked in debug builds. A size:: line with no value is legal Logseq and is exactly the SPEC 3.3 "present key, zero atoms" case, so the crash was reachable from an ordinary graph. The empty value now borrows the tail of its own line.

entries.title: A concord-ledger index or pin entry survived every prune once its blob was removed from outside the ledger

coverage.failBefore: cargo test -p tine-core --lib concord_ledger::tests::prune_reclaims with the two new match arms reverted: dangling_entries_removed 0, expected 3

entries.notes: prune() collected the hash named by each index and pin file and deleted only blobs nothing referenced, plus files that failed to parse. An entry whose blob had been removed from outside the ledger -- antivirus quarantine (the GH #411 reporter's case), a disk cleaner, a partial restore -- still parsed, so it was kept and its hash was even added to the referenced set. Every lookup through it already answered None, because base() verifies the blob's content hash, so no user-visible behaviour was wrong; the entry was simply dead metadata that accumulated and was re-read by every later prune. prune() now also removes index and pin files naming an absent blob. This is hygiene only: the ledger is disposable state that may never warn, refuse, or report a missing blob, so no diagnostic was added.
